> **Using ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini in a browser?** Copy this into the chat:
>
> ```
> I'm at SF x MIT Hack Day: Energy on Track [1, 2, 3 or 4]. Read
> https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arhamshah08/energy-hack/main/ai/START.md
> and then the file for my track. List the most relevant open tools, datasets and papers
> (with links) for: [your idea]. Prefer ones with no API key.
> ```

Everything a team and its AI agent need to go from an idea to a working demo by **18:30**:
four tracks, ready-made problems, 300+ datasets, open-source tools, simulators, papers and programs.
Grid prices (LMP), demand and fuel mix for every US ISO: [gridstatus.io](https://www.gridstatus.io/). California feeder capacity: [PG&E GRIP](https://grip.pge.com/).

## Pick a track

| | Track | The question | Start |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | Identify suitable sites | Where can distributed compute get power in months, not years? | [Open →](tracks/1-sites/README.md) |
| **2** | Assess grid capacity at the edge | How much power is there, and how soon? | [Open →](tracks/2-grid-capacity/README.md) |
| **3** | Manage loads | How can compute flex without breaking service? | [Open →](tracks/3-load-management/README.md) |
| **4** | Aggregate distributed compute | How do many sites act as one grid resource? | [Open →](tracks/4-aggregation/README.md) |

**Ideas around speed to power** (permitting layer for the grid, vision models reading city permits, AI plans to speed up approvals, Omniverse grid twins and more): [ideas](guides/ideas/README.md).

**Starter data**: hourly 2025 demand and generation by fuel for the 12 largest US grid operators, one line to load: [data](data/grid-hourly-2025/README.md).

Not sure? Browse the [RFQs](guides/rfq/README.md): 22 problems people have today, each sized for one day.

## Schedule

| Time | |
|---|---|
| 10:00 | Doors, coffee, intro |
| 10:30 | Team formation |
| 13:00 | Lunch |
| **18:30** | **Demos** ([ideas](guides/playbook/demo-template.md)) |
| 19:30 | Done |

## Use it with your agent

**Coding agents** (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI) read [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) automatically:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/arhamshah08/energy-hack
cd energy-hack
# open your agent here and tell it your track
```

**Chat agents** (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini in a browser): use the prompt at the top of this page. Each track has a
compact file with every resource on one line:
[Track 1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arhamshah08/energy-hack/main/ai/track-1-sites.md) ·
[Track 2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arhamshah08/energy-hack/main/ai/track-2-grid-capacity.md) ·
[Track 3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arhamshah08/energy-hack/main/ai/track-3-load-management.md) ·
[Track 4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arhamshah08/energy-hack/main/ai/track-4-aggregation.md) ·
[Open-source tools](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arhamshah08/energy-hack/main/ai/open-source-tools.md) ·
[Everything](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arhamshah08/energy-hack/main/ai/all-resources.md)

**Search the catalog** (Python 3, nothing to install):

```bash
python3 scripts/find.py --track 2 --access open     # no-key data for Track 2
python3 scripts/find.py --track 3 --kind paper      # papers for Track 3
python3 scripts/find.py --tag simulation            # simulators for any track
```

## The theme: grid-friendly compute

Compute that connects and runs without pushing the grid past its limits, and helps the grid when
it can. Any angle that gets there fits: simulation, self-improving agents (RSI), coordination
signals, edge AI workloads, forecasting, storage, onsite generation, EV charging and
vehicle-to-grid, grid-forming microgrids, cooling and water,
reliability, markets, carbon, permitting speed, community impact, and more.
[19 example angles with starting resources →](guides/theme/README.md)

## What is in the repo

| Folder | Contents |
|---|---|
| [`tracks/`](tracks) | One page per track, with all its resources |
| [`tools/`](tools/README.md) | 110+ free open-source tools, grouped by use |
| [`data/`](data/README.md) | Starter datasets, ready to load |
| [`guides/`](guides/README.md) | Ideas, ready-made problems, concepts, glossary |
| [`ai/`](ai/START.md) | Chat-ready files for ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini |
| [`catalog/`](catalog/SCHEMA.md) | All 320+ resources as YAML and JSON |
| [`scripts/`](scripts) | Search and build |

## Feedback

Anyone can share feedback, corrections or updates through the **[Energy Hack Repo Feedback form](https://forms.gle/k1pnQ4dtvfcGkuGK6)**:
participants, people who used the repo after the event, and the creators of any tool or project listed here
(tell us if a description, credit or link is wrong). Or email **arhams@stanford.edu**.

## Contribute

Found a useful resource during the day? Add one entry to `catalog/*.yaml` and open a pull request.
See [CONTRIBUTING.md](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md). Content CC BY 4.0, scripts MIT.



========== FILE: AGENTS.md ==========

# AGENTS.md

Instructions for any coding or chat agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini, ChatGPT,
Claude) helping a team at **SF x MIT Hack Day: Energy**, Sun 8 Nov 2026, AGI House SF.
Theme: **grid-friendly compute**. Demos at **18:30**.

## 1. Your job

Help the team ship a working, presentable result by 18:30 in one track, with a clear story of how
it expands. Output over exploration.

## 2. Start of session

| Step | Do |
|---|---|
| 1 | Ask which track: **1** sites, **2** grid capacity, **3** load management, **4** aggregation. If unsure, show [guides/rfq/README.md](guides/rfq/README.md) and the four track pages |
| 2 | Read the track page `tracks/<n>/README.md` |
| 3 | Help the team get a first result running quickly, then improve it |

## 3. Rules

1. **Stay in the team's track.** Pull resources from another track only when the team needs
   something it does not have; each track page has a "When you need another track" table.
2. **Aim for the 18:30 demo.** Favour a working result over a large unfinished one; if time
   runs short, suggest a smaller scope.
3. **Loops demo well.** If the team runs a propose, check, score, keep loop, log each iteration;
   an improvement chart shows the event's theme.
4. **Prefer open data.** Use `access: open` resources first. Flag anything needing a key,
   billing, a large download, a GPU, or MATLAB/Julia before the team commits to it.
5. **Do not choose the idea for them.** Offer 2 to 3 options from the ideas page, RFQs or catalog when asked;
   the team decides. Do push them to scope down.
6. **Cite catalog ids and URLs.** Never invent datasets, papers or numbers. Label anything from
   outside the catalog as not verified. Respect `status: preprint/unverified` and
   `link_check: blocks-bots` (works only in a browser).
7. **Label synthetic data** in outputs and the demo.
8. **Questions you cannot answer** about the repo or an RFQ: point the team to the feedback form or
   arhams@stanford.edu.

## 4. Feedback

Energy Hack Repo Feedback form, for participants, later users, and creators of listed tools who want to change their entry: https://forms.gle/k1pnQ4dtvfcGkuGK6
Or email arhams@stanford.edu. After the demo, or if the team finds a wrong link, credit or description, suggest they use it.

## 5. Schedule

Team formation 10:30, lunch 13:00, **demos 18:30**. Demo ideas: [guides/playbook/demo-template.md](guides/playbook/demo-template.md).

## 6. Finding resources

```bash
python3 scripts/find.py --track 2                    # everything for one track
python3 scripts/find.py --track 2 --access open      # no-key data for that track
python3 scripts/find.py --track 3 --kind paper       # papers for a track
python3 scripts/find.py --tag simulation             # simulators across tracks
python3 scripts/find.py --role harness               # RSI loop frameworks
python3 scripts/find.py --json --track 4             # machine-readable
```

No dependencies, Python 3.8+. Without a shell, read `ai/START.md` and the track file in `ai/` (one resource per line), or `catalog/catalog.json`.

## 7. Where things are

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `tracks/1-sites/` ... `tracks/4-aggregation/` | Problem, facts, loop options, demo formats, cross-track table, then all resources for the track (data, simulators, papers, programs) |
| `guides/ideas/README.md` | Ideas around speed to power (permitting layer, vision on permits, AI approval plans, Omniverse grid twins) |
| `data/` | Starter datasets, e.g. hourly 2025 grid demand and generation for 12 US operators |
| `guides/rfq/README.md` | Ready-made problems per track with starting data, verifier and demo output |
| `tools/` | Free tools grouped by use, with creators and licenses |
| `guides/concepts/` | Grid ideas explained (load flow, grid-forming microgrids, EV charging and V2G) with tools to try |
| `guides/theme/README.md` | Grid-friendly compute, 19 example angles (not a fixed list), angles by track |
| `guides/theme/rsi.md` | Recursive self-improvement: loop anatomy, known systems, failure modes |
| `guides/playbook/` | Schedule, demo ideas, copy-paste prompts |
| `guides/reference/` | Glossary, data setup cost, materials and fusion resources |
| `catalog/research/edge-compute/` | Raw deep research; read the source note (search its `ref`) before quoting a number |
| `catalog/*.yaml`, `catalog/catalog.json` | All resources. Schema: `catalog/SCHEMA.md` |

# Open-source tools

Free tools teams can use today, with credit to the people and organisations who built and share
them. Check each tool's license before reusing its code.

**Built one of these tools?** If a description, credit or link is wrong, or you want something added, tell us
through the [feedback form](https://forms.gle/k1pnQ4dtvfcGkuGK6) or email arhams@stanford.edu.

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED -->

_121 tools. Generated from the catalog by `scripts/build.py`._

## Try in the browser, no install

| Tool | Built by | What it does | Tracks | License |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Load Flow Simulator (browser)](https://tool.adjiebrotots.com/loadflow-simulator/) | Adjie Brotosukmono | Free browser tool: draw a single-line diagram and run AC Newton-Raphson or DC load flow (PyPSA-based), with animated flows. Examples include a 9-bus system, a 20/0.4 kV feeder and an HVDC link. Offers a link for AI agents to open a scenario. | 2 | Free web tool |
| [AC Grid Lab (browser AC power flow)](https://www.eshansingh.xyz/acopf/) | Dr. Eshan Singh | Browser tool: build a one-line network on a map or diagram and solve AC power flow; starter case is a California-inspired nine-bus network with voltage and line-loading checks. JSON import and export. | 2 | Free web tool |
| [ED/UC Simulator: economic dispatch and unit commitment (browser)](https://tool.adjiebrotots.com/ed-uc-simulator/) | Adjie Brotosukmono | Free browser tool: draw a network, decide which units run hour by hour and read nodal prices (LMP); PyPSA with the HiGHS solver. Examples include a PJM 5-bus case and solar plus battery. | 2, 3 | Free web tool |
| [PyPSA California: interactive grid model (browser)](https://www.eshansingh.xyz/PyPSA-CA/app/) | Dr. Eshan Singh | Browser app over a PyPSA optimization model of the California grid: configure demand, generation, storage, transmission and policy, then solve. No install. | 2, 3 | Free web tool |

## LF Energy projects (42)

Open-source energy projects hosted by [LF Energy](https://lfenergy.org/projects/), the Linux Foundation's energy foundation. Browse them all at https://lfenergy.org/projects/, for example [AINETUS](https://lfenergy.org/projects/ainetus/) (AI decision support for grid operators).

| [pandapower](https://github.com/e2nIEE/pandapower) | Fraunhofer IEE and University of Kassel | Python power flow and optimal power flow on pandas tables, with standard test networks. | 2 | See repo |
| [MATPOWER](https://github.com/MATPOWER/matpower) | MATPOWER team (Ray Zimmerman) | MATLAB/Octave power flow and OPF package. Its case format is used by most grid benchmarks. | - | See repo |
| [PowerModels.jl](https://github.com/lanl-ansi/PowerModels.jl) | Los Alamos National Laboratory | Julia package for steady-state power network optimization with many formulations. | - | See repo |
| [OpenDSSDirect.py](https://github.com/dss-extensions/OpenDSSDirect.py) | DSS-Extensions (OpenDSS by EPRI) | Python bindings for OpenDSS distribution system simulator. Used for feeder-level hosting capacity studies. | 2 | See repo |
| [GridLAB-D](https://github.com/gridlab-d/gridlab-d) | PNNL | Distribution system and end-use load simulator from PNNL, including responsive loads and markets. | 2, 4 | See repo |
| [PyPSA](https://github.com/PyPSA/PyPSA) | PyPSA team | Python power system optimization: capacity expansion, unit commitment and power flow. | 2 | MIT |
| [PyPSA-USA](https://github.com/PyPSA/pypsa-usa) | PyPSA-USA contributors | Open US power system model built on PyPSA with EIA and other public data. | 2 | MIT |
| [GridSFM: small foundation models for the power grid (Microsoft Research)](https://github.com/microsoft/GridSFM) | Microsoft Research | Microsoft Research framework for small foundation models in grid optimization, starting with AC optimal power flow. Learns from graph representations of topology, load, dispatch, flows and voltages across many scenarios. Open checkpoint (GridSFM_Open), datasets on Hugging Face, and an open-data pipeline from OpenStreetMap to solved OPF cases. Suited to fast screening (contingencies, planning scenarios, new data center load) and to giving exact solvers a starting point, not replacing them. MIT. | 2 | MIT |
| [ANDES: power system transient dynamics in Python (CURENT)](https://github.com/CURENT/andes) | CURENT (Hantao Cui et al.) | Python library for phasor-domain transient stability simulation with symbolic model definitions, including inverter-based resource models. See the repo for license. | 2, 4 | See repo |
| [Generic EMT Modeling of Data Center Load (Dartmouth)](https://github.com/xingyuz-phd/Generic-EMT-Modeling-of-Data-Center-Load) | Xingyu Zhao, Yingyi Tang, Junbo Zhao (Dartmouth) | Modular electromagnetic transient model of a data center fed by a centralized UPS: rectifier, inverter, battery DC-DC, PFC, buck and VFD modules at three fidelity levels, IT load profiles and voltage ride-through control. Needs PSCAD 5.0.2 (commercial). No license file in the repo; ask the authors before reusing code. | 2, 3 | None stated |
| [OpenIBR: open-source grid-forming controls](https://www.openibr.org/) | Heron Power | Universal grid-forming controller for inverter-based resources and large electronic loads such as data centers, aligned with IEEE 2800 and UNIFI. v1.1 builds IEEE/CIGRE TB958 DLLs from the open C code for PSCAD and similar tools, with debug outputs and a COMTRADE-logging test environment. Code: github.com/HeronPower/OpenIBR; DLL guide: github.com/HeronPower/OpenIBR/blob/dev/documentation/9_using_the_ieee_cigre_dll.md | 2, 3 | Apache-2.0 |
| [HELICS co-simulation framework](https://github.com/GMLC-TDC/HELICS) | US DOE Grid Modernization Lab Consortium (PNNL, LLNL, NREL) | Couples separate simulators (grid, buildings, markets, comms) into one time-synchronized federation. ========== FILE: guides/theme/README.md ==========

[← Front page](../../README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; [Feedback form](https://forms.gle/k1pnQ4dtvfcGkuGK6)

# Theme: grid-friendly compute

**Grid-friendly compute** connects and runs without pushing the grid past its limits, and helps
the grid when it can. In the sources in this repo that means five properties:

| # | Property | Track where it is worked on |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Located where power and network capacity exist | [Track 1 Sites](../../tracks/1-sites/README.md) |
| 2 | Sized to the headroom the local grid actually has | [Track 2 Grid capacity](../../tracks/2-grid-capacity/README.md) |
| 3 | Able to reduce, shift or smooth its load when the grid is stressed | [Track 3 Load management](../../tracks/3-load-management/README.md) |
| 4 | Coordinated across many sites so it acts as one resource the grid can rely on | [Track 4 Aggregation](../../tracks/4-aggregation/README.md) |
| 5 | Stays connected through grid faults instead of tripping together | Tracks 2 and 3 (`pjm-load-transfer-event-2026`, `ercot-ride-through-notice`) |

## 1. Why it matters now

| # | Fact | Source id |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | US data centers used about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023; 9.5% to 15.3% projected for 2030 | `lbnl-dc-energy-2024`, `lbnl-dc-energy-2025-update` |
| 2 | ERCOT tracked about 410 GW of large-load requests in March 2026, about 87% data centers | `ercot-legislative-update-2026` |
| 3 | Data centers build in 2 to 3 years; grid infrastructure generally takes longer | `iea-energy-ai-2025` |
| 4 | Nearly 100 GW of new load could use existing US capacity if it accepts limited curtailment (first-order estimate) | `duke-rethinking-load-growth-2025` |
| 5 | Nearly 4,000 MW of data center load tripped offline together in Virginia on 22 Jul 2026 | `pjm-load-transfer-event-2026` |
| 6 | Synchronized AI training swings power by tens of MW within seconds | `google-power-smoothing-2025` |
| 7 | Public hosting capacity maps are screening estimates, not commitments | `pge-ica`, `sce-drpep` |
| 8 | No single percentage of data center load is flexible; it depends on workload deadlines, design and program rules | `lbnl-integrating-ai-dc` |

More numbers and contested claims: [catalog/research/edge-compute](../../catalog/research/edge-compute/README.md).

## 2. Angles on the theme

Examples, not a fixed list. Any approach that makes compute easier on the grid fits. Bring your own angle.

| # | Angle | What it covers | Starting resources |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Simulation and digital twins** | Check an idea in a model before touching hardware, including Omniverse twins of a data center and its grid | `nvidia-omniverse-dsx`, `pandapower`, `sustaindc`, `energyplus`, `tamu-activsg10k` |
| 2 | **RSI and self-improving agents** | Loops that propose, check, score, keep, and get better each run ([rsi.md](rsi.md)) | `aideml`, `openevolve`, `dspy` |
| 3 | **Coordination and signals** | Prices, carbon, grid events, protocols between grid and compute | `openadr`, `openleadr`, `electricity-maps` |
| 4 | **Edge AI workloads** | Inference at small sites: latency, deadlines, power behaviour | `azure-llm-inference-traces`, `etsi-edge-native-2023`, `coral-npu` |
| 5 | **Forecasting** | Load, renewables, weather, prices, failures ahead of time | `surge-load-forecast`, `timecopilot`, `pravah` (India, on request), `pjm-historical-forecasts`, `eia-930`, `buildingsbench` |
| 6 | **Storage and batteries** | Batteries at or near compute to shave peaks or ride through events | `nrgise-open`, `bess-flexible-dispatch`, `pybamm`, `cec-dsgs-docket` |
| 7 | **Onsite generation and microgrids** | Solar, gas, microgrids serving compute | `nrel-reopt`, `nrel-sam`, `pge-redwood-microgrid` |
| 8 | **Cooling, heat and water** | Cooling energy, waste heat, water use | `energyplus`, `lbnl-water-use-workloads`, `jrc-eu-coc-2024` |
| 9 | **Reliability and ride-through** | Staying connected through faults; avoiding mass trips | `pjm-load-transfer-event-2026`, `ercot-ride-through-notice` |
| 10 | **Markets, prices and programs** | Who pays for flexibility and how to qualify | `gridstatus-io` (LMPs across US ISOs), `flex-pse` (Stanford), `caiso-demand-response`, `ercot-ers`, `openei-urdb` |
| 11 | **Carbon awareness** | Running work when and where the grid is cleaner | `watttime`, `carbon-aware-sdk`, `epa-egrid` |
| 12 | **Speed to power: interconnection and permitting** | Getting connected and approved sooner: a permitting layer for the grid, vision models reading city permits, AI plans for faster approval ([ideas](../ideas/README.md)) | `ercot-batch-zero`, `miso-firm-service-step-up`, `loudoun-dc-standards`, `sf-property-information-map` |
| 13 | **Community, cost and equity** | Bills, noise, jobs, local acceptance | `va-jlarc-2024`, `census-reporter-api` |
| 14 | **Measurement and verification** | Proving what was delivered: telemetry, metering | `kepler`, `miso-telemetry-pmu`, `caiso-dmm-dr-2024` |
| 15 | **Resilience and hazards** | Outages, wildfire, flood exposure | `eagle-i-outages`, `fema-nri`, `cpuc-fire-threat-map` |
| 16 | **Security and trust at the edge** | Multi-vendor edge sites and data between grid and compute | `etsi-mec-security-2022` |
| 17 | **EV smart charging and vehicle-to-grid** | Charging that follows grid signals; parked vehicles exporting power ([concept](../concepts/ev-smart-charging-v2g.md)) | `acn-data`, `acnportal`, `everest`, `ocpp` |
| 18 | **Grid-forming control and microgrids** | Batteries and onsite sources that island, share load and ride through ([concept](../concepts/grid-forming-microgrids.md)) | `openibr`, `andes`, `dc-emt-model`, `pge-redwood-microgrid` |
| 19 | **Grid physics** | Load flow, dispatch, stability ([concept](../concepts/load-flow.md)) | `loadflow-simulator-web`, `ac-grid-lab`, `ed-uc-simulator-web`, `pypsa-ca-app`, `pandapower` |

Four of these have searchable tags: `python3 scripts/find.py --tag simulation` (also `rsi`, `coordination`, `edge-ai`).

## 3. Some angles by track

Examples of how a few angles show up in each track. Explanations of grid ideas: [concepts](../concepts/README.md).

| | Simulation | RSI loop shape | Coordination | Edge AI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 Sites** | Site energy and onsite generation: `nrel-reopt`, `nrel-sam`, `nrel-rev` | Propose candidate locations; score them against data layers | Zoning, permits, utility process: `loudoun-dc-standards`, `santa-clara-zoning` | Latency and network reach: `peeringdb`, `ripe-atlas`, `fcc-broadband-map` |
| **2 Grid capacity** | Power flow and N-1 on synthetic grids: `tamu-activsg10k`, `pandapower`, `matpower` | Propose placements or splits of load; power flow scores violations | Large-load processes: `ercot-batch-zero`, `miso-firm-service-step-up`, `pjm-large-load-vetting` | AI load shape assumptions: `eia-aeo2026-servers` (flat) vs `google-power-smoothing-2025` (swings) |
| **3 Load management** | Data center workload, cooling and battery sims: `sustaindc`, `vessim`, `energyplus` | Propose schedules or control policies; simulator scores cost, carbon, delayed jobs | Price, carbon and DR signals: `electricity-maps`, `watttime`, `pge-business-dr` | Inference traces and power telemetry: `azure-llm-inference-traces`, `kepler` |
| **4 Aggregation** | Multi-site coordination sims: `citylearn`, `helics`, `gridlab-d` | Propose dispatch across sites; simulator scores delivered vs committed MW | Protocols and markets: `openadr`, `ieee-2030-5`, `ferc-2222`, `caiso-der-provider` | Workload mobility across edge sites: `etsi-edge-native-2023` |

========== FILE: guides/playbook/demo-template.md ==========

[← Front page](../../README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; [Feedback form](https://forms.gle/k1pnQ4dtvfcGkuGK6)

# Demo ideas (demos at 18:30)

A suggested shape, not a requirement.

## 1. Structure (about 3 minutes)

| # | Part | Time | Content |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Problem | 20 s | Track, the problem in one sentence, one number that shows why it matters (catalog has sourced numbers) |
| 2 | Approach | 30 s | Data, verifier, metric, loop. One diagram or one sentence each |
| 3 | Live result | 70 s | The output: map, chart, dashboard, before and after |
| 4 | Improvement | 20 s | Score across loop iterations: how the system got better each run |
| 5 | How it expands | 30 s | The next three steps (below) |
| 6 | Ask | 10 s | Data, partners or feedback you want |

## 2. How it expands

Pick the ones that fit and say them concretely.

| # | Direction | Example wording |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Real data | "Today on synthetic or sample data; next on utility or operator data" |
| 2 | Scale | "One region today; the same loop runs on any region in the catalog" |
| 3 | Fidelity | "Next: N-1 contingencies, hourly load, a full year" |
| 4 | Across tracks | "Our sites (Track 1) feed a capacity check (Track 2), then a flexibility plan (Track 3)" |
| 5 | Coordination | "Connect to real signals: OpenADR, prices, carbon" |
| 6 | Longer loops | "More iterations, better proposer, the loop improves its own search" |
| 7 | Users | "Who would run this weekly, and what decision it changes" |

## 3. Checklist

| # | Item |
|---|---|
| 1 | Demo runs offline or with cached data |
| 2 | Backup screen recording saved |
| 3 | Screenshots of the key output |
| 4 | Iteration log or improvement chart included |
| 5 | Sources cited for any number shown (catalog id or link) |
| 6 | Synthetic data labelled as synthetic |
| 7 | Repo or link ready to share |

# Prompts

Copy, paste, fill the brackets. Coding agents: run inside the cloned repo. Chat agents (ChatGPT,
Claude, Gemini in a browser): first paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arhamshah08/energy-hack/main/ai/START.md` and say your track.

## Explore the tracks

```
Read AGENTS.md and guides/rfq/README.md. We are a team of [N] with skills in [skills].
Summarise the four tracks in one line each and list RFQs that fit our skills and can run on
open data. Give 3 options with the data and simulator each needs; we will choose.
```

## Get started on a track

```
We are on Track [1-4] working on: [problem]. Read tracks/[folder]/README.md and suggest the
quickest open data and simulator to get a first result running. Flag anything that needs a key,
billing or a large download.
```

## Build a loop

```
Turn what we have into a loop: propose a change, check it with [simulator], score it, keep it if
better. Log each iteration to iterations.csv and plot the score over iterations.
```

## Borrow from another track

```
We are on Track [n] and need [what is missing]. Use the "When you need another track" table in
our track page and scripts/find.py to find the 3 most relevant resources.
```

## Prepare the demo

```
Using guides/playbook/demo-template.md, draft a short demo of what we built: the problem with one
sourced number, what we did, the result, and three concrete ways it could expand.
```

# Ideas: speed to power

**Speed to power** is the time from picking a site to having electricity flowing to it. For new
compute it is often the longest step: a data center can be built in 2 to 3 years, while grid
connections and approvals generally take longer (`iea-energy-ai-2025`). Generation projects wait a
median of over five years from request to operation (`lbnl-queued-up`), and towns are adding
moratoria and special permits for data centers (`richmond-dc-moratorium`, `loudoun-dc-standards`).

These are ideas, not assignments. Pick one, combine them, or bring your own.
More problem statements: [RFQs](../rfq/README.md).

## 1. Speed to power: permits and approvals

| # | Idea | What it does | Start with | Track |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | **Grid permitting layer** | A map layer for the grid that joins, per site: zoning and moratoria, permits already issued, utility hosting capacity, and large-load process status. Answers "how fast could this site get power?" | `sf-property-information-map`, `national-zoning-atlas`, filings (`--kind filing`), `pge-ica`, `ercot-batch-zero`, `va-deq-air-permits`, `nepa-mcp` | 1, 2 |
| 1.2 | **Vision to scan city permitting data** | Vision-language models read permit PDFs, council records, site plans and single-line diagrams, and turn them into structured data: requirements, conditions, decisions, dates | `santa-clara-planning-record`, `santa-clara-zoning`, `tulare-dc-moratorium` (CEQAnet records), `va-deq-air-permits`, `loudoun-dc-standards` | 1 |
| 1.3 | **AI plans to accelerate city approvals** | Given a site and the city's rules, an agent drafts the application checklist, pre-checks the plan against code, prepares answers to common conditions (noise, water, backup generators) and flags what usually slows approval | Same records as 1.2, `va-jlarc-2024` (noise, water, local impacts), `jrc-eu-coc-2024` | 1 |
| 1.4 | **Speed-to-power scorecard** | Combine permitting status, hosting capacity, grid process and onsite power options into an estimated time to energize, per site | 1.1 outputs, `pge-ica`, `nrel-reopt`, `miso-firm-service-step-up` | 1, 2 |
| 1.5 | **Connect sooner with flexibility** | Estimate how much earlier a site connects if it accepts limited curtailment or non-firm service | `duke-rethinking-load-growth-2025`, `miso-firm-service-step-up`, `starter-us-grid-hourly-2025`, `pandapower` | 2, 3 |

## 2. Digital twins and grid data

| # | Idea | What it does | Start with | Track |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | **Omniverse for grid data** | Use NVIDIA Omniverse (DSX Blueprint, OpenUSD) to build a digital twin of a data center and its local grid, feed it real hourly grid data, and test how the site responds to grid conditions (the DSX Flex idea) | `nvidia-omniverse-dsx`, `nvidia-dsx-announcement-2025`, `starter-us-grid-hourly-2025`, `tamu-activsg10k` | 2, 3 |
| 2.2 | **Grid twin without special hardware** | The same idea on open tools: synthetic grid plus hourly data plus power flow, viewed on a map | `tamu-activsg10k`, `pandapower`, `starter-us-grid-hourly-2025`, `ac-grid-lab` | 2 |
| 2.3 | **Live grid context for a site** | Show prices, demand and generation mix for the site's grid operator next to its load | `gridstatus-io`, `starter-us-grid-hourly-2025` | 2, 3 |

## 3. Flexible and coordinated compute

| # | Idea | What it does | Start with | Track |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | **Compute that follows the grid** | Shift flexible jobs to hours with spare capacity, low prices or clean power | `starter-us-grid-hourly-2025`, `google-cluster-data`, `flex-pse`, `lfe-flexmeasures` | 3 |
| 3.2 | **EVs and compute on one connection** | Schedule EV charging and compute together so a shared site stays under its limit; add vehicle-to-grid | `acn-data`, `acnportal`, [EV concept](../concepts/ev-smart-charging-v2g.md) | 3, 4 |
| 3.3 | **Ride-through instead of trip-off** | Show how a data center's power electronics could stay connected through faults | `openibr`, `dc-emt-model`, `pjm-load-transfer-event-2026` | 2, 3 |
| 3.4 | **Many small sites as one resource** | Answer a grid request across a fleet of edge sites and prove what was delivered | `lfe-flexmeasures`, `openleadr`, `open-satori`, `citylearn` | 4 |

## 4. Self-improving agents (RSI)

| # | Idea | What it does | Start with | Track |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.1 | **An agent that gets faster at siting** | Proposes sites, checks them against permitting and grid data, scores speed to power, and improves its search each run | [rsi.md](../theme/rsi.md), `openevolve`, `aideml`, ideas 1.1 and 1.4 | 1, 2 |
| 4.2 | **An agent that learns approval patterns** | Reads past permit decisions and learns which plan features lead to faster approval | Ideas 1.2 and 1.3 | 1 |

Have an idea to add? [Feedback form](https://forms.gle/k1pnQ4dtvfcGkuGK6) or arhams@stanford.edu.

# US grid demand and generation, hourly, 2025

Hourly demand and generation by fuel for the 12 largest US grid operators (balancing authorities),
for all of 2025. Cleaned from US EIA Form 930, ready to load in one line. Public domain (US government data).

| File | Size | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| [us_grid_hourly_2025.csv](us_grid_hourly_2025.csv) | 13.8 MB, 105,120 rows | One row per operator per hour |
| [us_grid_summary_2025.csv](us_grid_summary_2025.csv) | 2 KB | One row per operator: annual demand, peak, generation mix |

## Load it

```python
import pandas as pd
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arhamshah08/energy-hack/main/data/grid-hourly-2025/us_grid_hourly_2025.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(url, parse_dates=["utc_time_end"])
ercot = df[df.ba == "ERCO"]                       # one operator
ercot.plot(x="utc_time_end", y=["demand_mw", "solar_mw", "wind_mw"])
```

## Operators included

| Code | Operator | Region |
|---|---|---|
| CISO | California ISO (CAISO) | California |
| ERCO | ERCOT | Texas |
| PJM | PJM Interconnection | Mid-Atlantic and Midwest |
| MISO | Midcontinent ISO | Midwest |
| NYIS | New York ISO | New York |
| ISNE | ISO New England | New England |
| SWPP | Southwest Power Pool | Central |
| BPAT | Bonneville Power Administration | Northwest |
| DUK | Duke Energy Carolinas | Carolinas |
| SOCO | Southern Company | Southeast |
| TVA | Tennessee Valley Authority | Tennessee |
| FPL | Florida Power & Light | Florida |

## Columns (hourly file)

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ba`, `ba_name`, `region` | Operator code, name, EIA region |
| `utc_time_end`, `local_time_end` | End of the hour, UTC and local (values are hourly averages, hour-ending) |
| `demand_forecast_mw` | Operator's day-ahead demand forecast |
| `demand_mw` | Demand (EIA adjusted series) |
| `net_generation_mw` | Total net generation (adjusted) |
| `interchange_mw` | Net flow out of the area; negative means importing |
| `coal_mw` ... `unknown_mw` | Net generation by source (adjusted). `solar_mw` and `wind_mw` include units with integrated batteries; `battery_mw` is stand-alone storage (negative when charging) |

## 2025 at a glance (from the summary file)

| Operator | Demand (TWh) | Peak (MW) | Largest sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| PJM | 843 | 160,560 | Gas 42%, nuclear 31%, coal 17% |
| MISO | 664 | 120,343 | Gas 35%, coal 29%, wind 15% |
| ERCOT | 487 | 83,597 | Gas 41%, wind 23%, solar 14% |
| SPP | 300 | 54,411 | Wind 37%, coal 29%, gas 25% |
| CAISO | 224 | 43,860 | Gas 40%, solar 25%, hydro 11% |

## Things to know

| # | Note |
|---|---|
| 1 | Operator areas are balancing authorities, not states; some utilities inside a state run their own area |
| 2 | "Adjusted" values are EIA's cleaned series, with some gaps filled by imputation |
| 3 | Battery storage is reported as its own source from 2025 |
| 4 | No prices or emissions in this file; prices: `gridstatus-io`, emissions: `epa-egrid` |
| 5 | Other operators and years: EIA bulk files at https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/ (`eia-930`) |

Rebuild: `scripts/data/make_grid_dataset.py`. Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-930.

========== FILE: guides/concepts/load-flow.md ==========

[← Front page](../../README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; [Concepts](README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; [Feedback form](https://forms.gle/k1pnQ4dtvfcGkuGK6)

# Load flow (power flow)

**Used most in:** [Track 2 Grid capacity](../../tracks/2-grid-capacity/README.md), also Tracks 1 and 3.

## 1. What it is

Load flow calculates the voltage at every node (bus) and the active power, reactive power and
current on every line and transformer of a network, for one steady-state operating condition.
It answers the basic grid question: **can this network carry this generation and demand within
its physical and regulatory limits?** Every grid connection offer for a large load, battery or
generator rests on load flow studies.

## 2. Inputs and outputs

| In | Out |
|---|---|
| Network topology: which buses connect to which | Voltage magnitude and angle at every bus |
| Impedance of every line and transformer | Active power (MW) on every branch |
| Transformer tap positions | Reactive power (MVAr) on every branch |
| Generation and demand at every bus | Losses (I²R heat in conductors and transformers) |
| Voltage set points of generators | Loading of each branch as % of its rating |

Each bus is one of three types:

| Bus type | Fixed | Solved for | Typical |
|---|---|---|---|
| Slack (reference) | Voltage magnitude and angle | P and Q | One large generator or the grid connection point; balances losses |
| PV | Active power P and voltage magnitude | Q and angle | Generators and inverters controlling voltage |
| PQ | Active power P and reactive power Q | Voltage magnitude and angle | Loads, including a data center |

## 3. How it is solved

| Method | What it does | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| AC power flow (Newton-Raphson) | Solves the full nonlinear equations iteratively | Voltage and reactive power matter; final checks |
| Fast decoupled | Approximation of Newton-Raphson that separates P-angle from Q-voltage | Large networks, faster iterations |
| DC power flow | Linear approximation: flat voltages, no reactive power, no losses | Fast screening of thermal limits across many cases; inside optimization loops |
| Optimal power flow (OPF) | Adds an objective, usually lowest cost, subject to network limits | Dispatch and pricing questions |
| Economic dispatch and unit commitment | Which units run and how much, hour by hour, and the resulting nodal prices | Market and operations questions (`ed-uc-simulator-web`) |
| Capacity expansion | What to build over years, then how to run it | Planning questions (`genx`, `pypsa`, `manta`; California in the browser: `pypsa-ca-app`) |
| Learned surrogate | Neural network trained to approximate AC power flow or OPF | Thousands of fast evaluations; check final answers with a real solver (`microsoft-gridsfm`) |

## 4. Limits it checks

| Limit | Typical value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Voltage at customer service (US) | ANSI C84.1 Range A: ±5% of nominal | Range B (wider) is allowed briefly |
| Transmission planning voltage | Often 0.95 to 1.05 per unit normal, about 0.90 to 1.10 after an outage | Criteria vary by utility and region |
| Thermal rating | Normal and short-term emergency ratings per line and transformer | Ratings can vary with season and weather |
| N-1 | All limits must hold with any single element out of service | Run one load flow per contingency |

Other countries use different limits; for example, some European distribution codes allow ±10%
at medium voltage.

## 5. What load flow does not capture

Load flow is steady state. Questions about what happens in the milliseconds and seconds after a
change need other studies:

| Study | Question | Open resource |
|---|---|---|
| Short circuit / fault level | How much current flows in a fault, can breakers clear it | `pandapower` (short circuit module) |
| Transient stability | Do generators and inverters stay in step after a disturbance | `andes` |
| Electromagnetic transients (EMT) | Fast power electronics behaviour: converters, UPS, ride-through | `dc-emt-model` (data center UPS load in PSCAD) |
| Harmonics | Distortion from power electronics | Specialist tools |
| Time series (quasi-static) | Load flow repeated for every hour of a year | `pandapower` timeseries, `opendssdirect` |

The July 2026 Virginia event (`pjm-load-transfer-event-2026`), where nearly 4,000 MW of data
center load disconnected together, is a dynamic problem: load flow alone would not show it.

## 6. Why it matters for grid-friendly compute

| # | Use |
|---|---|
| 1 | **Hosting capacity:** add MW at a bus until the first voltage or thermal violation |
| 2 | **Siting:** compare one large connection with the same load split across several buses |
| 3 | **Flexibility value:** see how many violations disappear if load drops in the binding hours |
| 4 | **Connection cost and curtailment:** violations drive network upgrades (cost) or limits on operation (curtailment), both of which flow into a project's finances |

## 7. Try it

In the browser, no install: draw a one-line diagram and run AC or DC load flow with the
[Load Flow Simulator](https://tool.adjiebrotots.com/loadflow-simulator/) by Adjie Brotosukmono (`loadflow-simulator-web`).
Or [AC Grid Lab](https://www.eshansingh.xyz/acopf/) by Dr. Eshan Singh (`ac-grid-lab`), which starts from a California-inspired nine-bus network.
For dispatch and prices: [ED/UC Simulator](https://tool.adjiebrotots.com/ed-uc-simulator/) by Adjie Brotosukmono (`ed-uc-simulator-web`).
For California-wide planning: [PyPSA California](https://www.eshansingh.xyz/PyPSA-CA/app/) by Dr. Eshan Singh (`pypsa-ca-app`).
All free tools, with credits: [open-source-tools](../../tools/README.md).

In Python, five lines:

```python
import pandapower as pp, pandapower.networks as pn
net = pn.case118()                                     # IEEE 118-bus test system
pp.create_load(net, bus=50, p_mw=100, q_mvar=20)        # add a 100 MW data center
pp.runpp(net)                                          # AC power flow
print(net.res_bus.vm_pu.min(), net.res_line.loading_percent.max())
```

Larger, map-based networks: `tamu-activsg10k`. Distribution feeders: `opendssdirect`.
Other solvers: `matpower`, `pypsa`, `powermodels`, and from LF Energy `lfe-powsybl` and `lfe-power-grid-model`.



========== FILE: guides/concepts/grid-forming-microgrids.md ==========

[← Front page](../../README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; [Concepts](README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; [Feedback form](https://forms.gle/k1pnQ4dtvfcGkuGK6)

# Grid-forming inverters and microgrid control

**Used most in:** [Track 3 Load management](../../tracks/3-load-management/README.md) and
[Track 4 Aggregation](../../tracks/4-aggregation/README.md); also ride-through questions in Track 2.

## 1. Why it matters here

Data centers increasingly sit behind batteries, UPS systems and onsite generation (IEA projects
20 to 25 GW of batteries at data centers by 2030, `iea-key-questions-2026`). All of these connect
through inverters. How those inverters are controlled decides whether a site can run as an
island, share load between sources, ride through grid disturbances, and help the grid instead of
tripping off with everyone else.

## 2. Grid-following vs grid-forming

| | Grid-following (GFL) | Grid-forming (GFM) |
|---|---|---|
| Behaves like | A controlled current source | A controlled voltage source |
| Needs an existing grid voltage | Yes, it locks onto it with a phase-locked loop | No, it sets voltage and frequency itself |
| Can run an island alone | No | Yes |
| Response to disturbances | Follows the grid; can lose sync in weak grids | Resists change; can provide inertia-like support |
| Typical today | Most solar and battery inverters | Growing in batteries and microgrids |

## 3. Control hierarchy in an islanded microgrid

Several grid-forming inverters in parallel need a clear split between fast and slow control.

| Layer | Speed | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Primary (each inverter) | about 5 to 15 ms | Droop, virtual impedance, power filtering: share load autonomously and keep the system stable |
| Secondary (site controller) | about 50 to 300 ms | Measure V, f, P, Q at the common bus and slowly restore voltage and frequency to target |
| Tertiary (energy management) | seconds to hours | Dispatch, state of charge, tariffs, grid programs, reconnection |

**Bandwidth separation** is the key design rule: each layer must be much slower than the one
below it, so the site controller corrects real deviations without fighting the inverters.

## 4. The building blocks

**Droop control** lets parallel sources share load with no fast communication. Each inverter
lowers its frequency as its active power rises and lowers its voltage as its reactive power rises:

```
f = f_ref - n_f * P
V = V_ref - m_v * Q
```

Because all inverters see the same frequency, they settle where each carries power in inverse
proportion to its droop slope. The cost is a small, deliberate deviation in f and V, which the
secondary layer later removes.

**Virtual impedance** makes the inverter act as if it had a chosen output impedance. It improves
reactive power sharing, reduces circulating current between parallel inverters, lowers sensitivity
to unequal cable and transformer impedances, and adds damping. Droop sets the sharing rule;
virtual impedance makes the sharing behave well through the real network.

**Power filtering and virtual inertia.** Measured P and Q are filtered so droop does not chase
every transient, harmonic or measurement blip. Slowing the response this way also gives an
inertia-like behaviour: frequency changes more gently after a step in load. Virtual synchronous
machine (VSM) controls make this explicit by emulating a rotating machine's inertia and damping.

**Site controller.** Watches the common point (for example the medium-voltage bus) and nudges each
inverter's V_ref and f_ref to bring the system back to nominal, then hands over to energy
management for slower decisions.

The goal, in order: stable sharing, controlled transient response, coordinated restoration,
robust steady state.

## 5. Links to data center loads

| # | Point | Source id |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | AI training swings tens of MW within seconds; inverters and storage can smooth it | `google-power-smoothing-2025` |
| 2 | Large loads tripping together is a reliability risk; ride-through behaviour depends on UPS and converter controls | `pjm-load-transfer-event-2026`, `ercot-ride-through-notice` |
| 3 | A data center's UPS and converters can be modelled in EMT to study grid interactions | `dc-emt-model` |
| 4 | Open grid-forming controls now exist for large electronic loads such as data centers, not only for generators | `openibr` |
| 5 | A measured community microgrid: battery, PV, islanding events, controls lessons | `pge-redwood-microgrid` |

## 6. Simulate it

| Tool | Level | Id |
|---|---|---|
| Dynawo (LF Energy) | Power system dynamics with power-electronic resources | `lfe-dynawo` |
| OpenIBR | Open grid-forming controller for inverters and large electronic loads; TB958 DLLs for PSCAD (Heron Power) | `openibr` |
| ANDES (Python) | Phasor-domain transient stability, including inverter-based resource models | `andes` |
| PSCAD data center model | EMT, data center UPS and converters (commercial PSCAD) | `dc-emt-model` |
| HELICS | Couple a grid simulator with a control or compute simulator | `helics` |
| pandapower | Steady-state check of the microgrid network | `pandapower` |
| NRGISE Open | Time-step simulation of a site's PV, storage and control strategy | `nrgise-open` |
| BESS dispatch optimizer | Battery schedule under changing grid export limits | `bess-flexible-dispatch` |



========== FILE: guides/concepts/ev-smart-charging-v2g.md ==========

[← Front page](../../README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; [Concepts](README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; [Feedback form](https://forms.gle/k1pnQ4dtvfcGkuGK6)

# EV smart charging and vehicle-to-grid

**Used most in:** [Track 3 Load management](../../tracks/3-load-management/README.md) and
[Track 4 Aggregation](../../tracks/4-aggregation/README.md).

## 1. What it is

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Smart charging (V1G) | Charging power is shifted or reduced in response to prices, grid events or site limits; energy flows one way |
| Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) | A bidirectional charger lets the vehicle battery export power back to the grid |
| V2B / V2H | Export to a building or home instead of the grid, behind the meter |
| Grid-interactive charging | Charging that receives grid signals and responds, whether one-way or bidirectional |

## 2. Why it fits grid-friendly compute

| # | Point |
|---|---|
| 1 | EV chargers and compute are both large, partly flexible loads that often share a site, a feeder and a connection limit |
| 2 | Charging can be scheduled around compute peaks so the site stays under its contracted or hosting capacity |
| 3 | Parked fleets (depots, workplaces) are batteries on wheels that can be aggregated alongside compute sites |
| 4 | The same coordination stack applies: price or event signals, a controller, measurement of what was delivered |

## 3. How chargers are controlled

| Layer | Standard | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Charger to management system | OCPP (Open Charge Point Protocol) | Start, stop and set charging limits; smart charging profiles (`ocpp`) |
| Vehicle to charger | ISO 15118 (part 20 adds bidirectional power) | Plug and charge, scheduling, power transfer negotiation (`iso-15118-20`) |
| Utility or aggregator to site | OpenADR, IEEE 2030.5 | Price and event signals (`openadr`, `ieee-2030-5`; open-source 2030.5 client: `open-satori`) |
| Bidirectional charger to grid | IEEE 1547 interconnection | Exporting chargers are treated as distributed energy resources (`ieee-1547`) |

## 4. Data and tools

| Resource | What it gives you | Id |
|---|---|---|
| ACN-Data (Caltech) | Real charging sessions: arrival, departure, energy delivered | `acn-data` |
| acnportal / ACN-Sim | Simulator for scheduling many chargers under a site capacity limit | `acnportal` |
| EVerest | Open-source charger software stack (OCPP, ISO 15118) | `everest` |
| CitrineOS | Open-source charger network management for OCPP 2.0.1 (LF Energy) | `lfe-citrineos` |
| AFDC station locator | US public charging stations with an API | `afdc-stations` |
| EVI-X toolbox | Models of charging demand and infrastructure needs | `evi-x-toolbox` |
| CPUC transportation electrification | California EV programs and rules | `cpuc-transportation-electrification` |

## 5. Questions to explore

See [RFQ 3.6 and 4.6](../rfq/README.md).



========== FILE: tracks/1-sites/README.md ==========

[← Front page](../../README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; Tracks: [1 Sites](../1-sites/README.md) · [2 Grid capacity](../2-grid-capacity/README.md) · [3 Load management](../3-load-management/README.md) · [4 Aggregation](../4-aggregation/README.md) · [RFQs](../../guides/rfq/README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; [Feedback form](https://forms.gle/k1pnQ4dtvfcGkuGK6)

# Track 1: Identify suitable sites

> Identify suitable sites for edge compute.

Theme link: grid-friendly compute starts with location. See [theme](../../guides/theme/README.md).

## 1. The problem

Hyperscale data centers (1 GW and up) can wait years for power. Large-load requests far outrun
approvals: ERCOT counted 238.6 GW of requests against 7.5 GW approved to energize since 2022
(`ercot-constraints-2025`), and new generation waits a median of more than five years from request
to operation (`lbnl-queued-up`).

**How can we bring power to GPUs in months or weeks instead of years?**

One path is the capacity that already exists across the distribution grid. Many feeders and
substations have spare room for **distributed compute** (`pge-ica`, `sce-drpep`), sized below where
large-load rules begin (25 MW in ERCOT, `ercot-nprr1234`).

Track 1 asks where those sites are. A good site has spare grid capacity nearby, clears land use and
permits, reaches fiber, avoids hazards, has cooling and water options, and sits near the users it
serves. Public data covers each layer separately. Joining them into a list of sites that can get
power fast is the work. More on speed to power: [ideas](../../guides/ideas/README.md).

## 2. Facts that shape this track

| # | Fact | Source id |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Local land use is changing fast: moratoria (Richmond to 2028, Tulare), Conditional Use Permits (Santa Clara), Special Exception (Loudoun) | `richmond-dc-moratorium`, `santa-clara-zoning`, `loudoun-dc-standards` |
| 2 | Zoning data is fragmented; no national field says "data center allowed" | `national-zoning-atlas` |
| 3 | Broadband maps show provider-reported service, not fiber routes, capacity or latency | `fcc-broadband-map` |
| 4 | Measured latency exists only between probes and targets | `ripe-atlas` |
| 5 | Workload water use varies by more than four orders of magnitude with cooling, climate and grid | `lbnl-water-use-workloads` |
| 6 | Backup generators need air permits; Virginia publishes them | `va-deq-air-permits` |
| 7 | A data center can take 2 to 3 years to build; grid connection often takes longer | `iea-energy-ai-2025` |

## 3. Your loop in this track

| Loop part | Options in the catalog |
|---|---|
| Data layers | `pge-ica` (PG&E GRIP for California, https://grip.pge.com/), `overpass-api`, `openinframap`, `eia-860`, `peeringdb`, `census-reporter-api`, `fema-nri`, `fema-nfhl`, `usgs-water-data`, `open-meteo`, `microsoft-us-building-footprints`, `national-zoning-atlas` |
| Verifier (check a site) | `nrel-reopt` (onsite energy), `pvlib-python` (onsite solar), `nrel-rev` (resource and exclusions), power flow at the nearest substation (Track 2) |
| Metric | Distance to substation and fiber, latency to users, hazard exposure, land and power cost, permit status |
| Proposer | A model or search that suggests candidate locations |

## 4. Outputs that demo well

| # | Format |
|---|---|
| 1 | Map with candidate sites coloured by score, click for the evidence behind the score |
| 2 | Ranked table of sites with each layer's contribution |
| 3 | Chart of score improvement across loop iterations |

========== FILE: tracks/2-grid-capacity/README.md ==========

[← Front page](../../README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; Tracks: [1 Sites](../1-sites/README.md) · [2 Grid capacity](../2-grid-capacity/README.md) · [3 Load management](../3-load-management/README.md) · [4 Aggregation](../4-aggregation/README.md) · [RFQs](../../guides/rfq/README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; [Feedback form](https://forms.gle/k1pnQ4dtvfcGkuGK6)

# Track 2: Assess grid capacity at the edge

> Assess grid capacity for edge compute.

Theme link: grid-friendly compute is sized to the headroom the local grid has. See [theme](../../guides/theme/README.md).

## 1. The problem

How much load can a location take, how soon, and under what conditions? Capacity is set by
transmission and distribution limits, by outages (N-1), and by the processes utilities and grid
operators use to approve large loads. Real network models are restricted, so public work uses
utility maps, ISO reports and synthetic grids.

## 2. Facts that shape this track

| # | Fact | Source id |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Detailed real grid models are restricted (CEII); public studies use synthetic grids | `ferc-ceii`, `tamu-synthetic-grids` |
| 2 | The western US synthetic grid has substation coordinates and an N-1 contingency list, but no hourly load | `tamu-activsg10k` |
| 3 | Utility hosting capacity maps are screening estimates, not commitments; PG&E gives 576 hourly values per line section | `pge-ica`, `pge-grip-guide`, `sce-drpep` |
| 4 | ERCOT: 238.6 GW of large-load requests vs 7.5 GW approved to energize since Jan 2022 | `ercot-constraints-2025` |
| 5 | PJM has no load queue; utilities submit large-load forecast adjustments that PJM vets | `pjm-large-load-vetting` |
| 6 | MISO is designing non-firm and step-up firm service so loads can connect before all upgrades | `miso-firm-service-step-up`, `miso-large-load-integration` |
| 7 | Large loads tripping together is now a planning concern; ride-through data is requested | `pjm-load-transfer-event-2026`, `ercot-ride-through-notice` |
| 8 | Power flow answers whether the network carries a load; production cost and capacity expansion models answer other questions | `pandapower`, `pypsa` |

## 3. Your loop in this track

| Loop part | Options in the catalog |
|---|---|
| Data | `gridstatus-io` (LMP, demand, fuel mix across all US ISOs, https://www.gridstatus.io/), `pge-ica` (PG&E GRIP, https://grip.pge.com/), `tamu-activsg10k`, `tamu-activsg2000`, `pge-grip-guide`, `sce-ica-featureserver`, `eia-930`, `gridstatus`, `pjm-historical-forecasts`, `surge-load-forecast`, `pravah` (grid weather forecasting for India, access on request: arhams@stanford.edu) |
| Verifier | `loadflow-simulator-web`, `ac-grid-lab`, `pypsa-ca-app` (browser, no install), `lfe-powsybl`, `lfe-power-grid-model`, `lfe-dynawo` (LF Energy), `pandapower`, `matpower`, `microsoft-gridsfm` (fast AC-OPF surrogate), `andes` (dynamics), `dc-emt-model` (data center EMT), `openibr` (grid-forming controls), `opendssdirect`, `gridlab-d`, `pypsa`, `pypsa-usa` |
| Metric | MW added before a thermal or voltage violation, violations under N-1, forecast error |
| Proposer | A model or search that suggests where and how much load to add, or how to split it |

## 4. Outputs that demo well

| # | Format |
|---|---|
| 1 | Map of buses or feeders coloured by remaining headroom |
| 2 | Before and after: violations with load at one bus vs spread across several |
| 3 | Headroom by hour of day or season |
| 4 | Chart of headroom found across loop iterations |

| `lfe-compas` | [CoMPAS](https://lfenergy.org/projects/compas/) | open | tool |  | Shared software blocks for IEC 61850 profile configuration in digital substations. LF Energy stage: Early Adoption. Code: github.com/com-pas. |
| `lfe-dynawo` | [Dynawo](https://lfenergy.org/projects/dyna%CF%89o/) | open | simulator |  | Simulation suite for power system dynamics: voltage, frequency, short circuit and stability with power-electronic resources and HVDC. Code: github.com/dynawo. |
| `lfe-energnn` | [EnerGNN](https://lfenergy.org/projects/energnn/) | open | tool |  | Graph neural network stack (H2MG) for amortized optimization: trained once on many grid cases, it returns near-instant solutions to new ones. LF Energy stage: Sandbox. Code: github.com/energnn/energnn. |
| `lfe-fidopower` | [FIDOpower](https://lfenergy.org/projects/fidopower/) | open | tool |  | Notebook-based tools for reproducible power system analysis. LF Energy stage: Sandbox. Code: github.com/fidopower. |
| `genx` | [GenX capacity expansion model (MIT, Princeton)](https://github.com/GenXProject/GenX.jl) | open | simulator |  | Julia model that chooses which generation, storage and transmission to build and how to operate it, for low-carbon power system studies. GPL-2.0. Needs Julia and a solver. |
| `microsoft-gridsfm` | [GridSFM: small foundation models for the power grid (Microsoft Research)](https://github.com/microsoft/GridSFM) | open | simulator |  | Microsoft Research framework for small foundation models in grid optimization, starting with AC optimal power flow. Learns from graph representations of topology, load, dispatch, flows and voltages across many scenarios. Open checkpoint (GridSFM_Open), datasets on Hugging Face, and an open-data pipeline from OpenStreetMap to solved OPF cases. Suited to fast screening (contingencies, planning scenarios, new data center load) and to giving exact solvers a starting point, not replacing them. MIT. |
| `loadflow-simulator-web` | [Load Flow Simulator (browser)](https://tool.adjiebrotots.com/loadflow-simulator/) | open | tool |  | Free browser tool: draw a single-line diagram and run AC Newton-Raphson or DC load flow (PyPSA-based), with animated flows. Examples include a 9-bus system, a 20/0.4 kV feeder and an HVDC link. Offers a link for AI agents to open a scenario. |
| `manta` | [Manta: open energy system modelling platform](https://manta-plan.org/) | open | tool |  | Open-source application for energy system modelling with graphical no-code workflows and full customization; plug-ins for PyPSA, GenX, Sienna and other frameworks; runs in the cloud, locally or on-premise; AI-assisted setup, debugging and results exploration. Code: github.com/manta-plan/manta (Apache-2.0). Launched 2026; public roadmap and beta program. |
| `opendssdirect` | [OpenDSSDirect.py](https://github.com/dss-extensions/OpenDSSDirect.py) | open | simulator |  | Python bindings for OpenDSS distribution system simulator. Used for feeder-level hosting capacity studies. |

Example data from the German market. No clear license in the repo; ask before reusing code. |

Searchable map of planned, under-construction, operating and retired power plants, batteries, data centers, large loads, lines and substations in the US and GB, plus energy RFPs and funding, built from interconnection queues, EIA-860M and permit registers with every record linked to its source. Phase 2 (plan approved 16 Sep 2025) covers data center and substation standards. Includes existing/proposed data center map. |

========== FILE: tracks/3-load-management/README.md ==========

[← Front page](../../README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; Tracks: [1 Sites](../1-sites/README.md) · [2 Grid capacity](../2-grid-capacity/README.md) · [3 Load management](../3-load-management/README.md) · [4 Aggregation](../4-aggregation/README.md) · [RFQs](../../guides/rfq/README.md) &nbsp;·&nbsp; [Feedback form](https://forms.gle/k1pnQ4dtvfcGkuGK6)

# Track 3: Manage loads

> Manage compute loads so they are grid-friendly.

Theme link: grid-friendly compute reduces, shifts or smooths its load when the grid is stressed. See [theme](../../guides/theme/README.md).

## 1. The problem

When and how can compute change its power draw without breaking service? Options include moving
jobs in time or place, capping power, using batteries or onsite generation, adjusting cooling, and
smoothing fast swings from AI training. Each option has a cost in delay, energy or reliability.

## 2. Facts that shape this track

| # | Fact | Source id |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Four flexibility mechanisms: compute shifting (time, place), facility infrastructure, storage, onsite generation | `lbnl-integrating-ai-dc` |
| 2 | Google shifts non-urgent work by site and hour when grid events are called; no MW series published | `google-dr-2023`, `google-dc-demand-response-2025` |
| 3 | A 2025 field demo cut an AI cluster's power 25% for 3 hours with software only (preprint) | `emerald-phoenix-2025` |
| 4 | Synchronized ML jobs swing tens of MW within seconds; smoothing cut swings about 50% for under 1% slowdown | `google-power-smoothing-2025` |
| 5 | Demand response was 2.6% of CAISO resource adequacy capacity in summer 2024 | `caiso-dmm-dr-2024` |
| 6 | Average and marginal carbon signals give different answers for load shifting | `watttime`, `electricity-maps` |
| 7 | Public inference traces have timestamps and token counts, not power or deadlines | `azure-llm-inference-traces` |

## 3. Your loop in this track

| Loop part | Options in the catalog |
|---|---|
| Data | `gridstatus-io` (prices and demand across all US ISOs, https://www.gridstatus.io/), `google-cluster-data` (incl. power traces), `azure-llm-inference-traces`, `alibaba-clusterdata`, `eia-930`, `caiso-todays-outlook`, `openei-urdb`, `epri-dcflex-deliverables` |
| Verifier | `flex-pse` (Stanford), `lfe-flexmeasures`, `lfe-openstef` (LF Energy), `sustaindc`, `vessim`, `nrgise-open`, `bess-flexible-dispatch`, `surge-load-forecast`, `timecopilot`, `pvlib-python`, `energyplus`, `carbon-aware-sdk`, `nrel-reopt` |
| Metric | MW reduced and for how long, delayed or dropped jobs, energy cost, emissions, peak demand charge, swing size |
| Proposer | A model, policy or LLM that proposes schedules, caps or setpoints |

**Featured:** [FlexMeasures](https://github.com/FlexMeasures/flexmeasures) by [Seita](https://seita.nl/) (Nicolas Höning), an open-source engine that schedules flexible loads, batteries and generation against prices and grid limits.
[flex-pse](https://github.com/flex-pse/flex-pse), from Stanford, schedules a facility's
energy use against real tariffs and demand response signals. Interested? Join the
[flex-pse Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/flex-pse/shared_invite/zt-4b2va6ztg-K74JiAdHsmqY2CoGjbOmIQ).

## 4. Outputs that demo well

| # | Format |
|---|---|
| 1 | Load curve before and after, with the grid event or price shown |
| 2 | Trade-off chart: MW reduced vs jobs delayed |
| 3 | Policy score across loop iterations (cost, carbon, delay) |

| Ready-to-load hourly grid data for shifting studies | [starter data](../../data/grid-hourly-2025/README.md) (`starter-us-grid-hourly-2025`) |

| `gridstatus` | [gridstatus (Python library)](https://github.com/gridstatus/gridstatus) | open | 2 | Python API for load, prices, fuel mix and queue data from US ISOs (CAISO, ERCOT, PJM, MISO, SPP, NYISO, ISO-NE). |
| `openleadr` | [OpenLEADR (OpenADR 2.0b in Python)](https://github.com/OpenLEADR/openleadr-python) | open | 4 | LF Energy project with open-source OpenADR implementations: openleadr-python (OpenADR 2.0b VEN and VTN, developmental) and openleadr-rs (Rust, OpenADR 3). Code: github.com/openleadr. |
| `pravah` | Pravah: weather forecasting for the grid (India) (access on request) | on-request | 2 | Weather forecasting built for power grid operations in India. Not public: access on request. Email arhams@stanford.edu for a contact. |
| `dersec-py1815` | [py1815: open IEEE 1815 (DNP3) outstation](https://github.com/DERSecurity/py1815) | open | 4 | The DNP3 (IEEE 1815) outstation of Project Satori, for distributed energy resources. Companion to the py20305 IEEE 2030.5 client. |
| `pysunspec2` | [pySunSpec2: SunSpec Modbus library](https://github.com/sunspec/pysunspec2) | open | 4 | Python library for reading and controlling SunSpec Modbus devices such as inverters and batteries. Model definitions at github.com/sunspec/models. Used as the Modbus bridge in Project Satori. |
| `open-satori` | [Satori: open IEEE 2030.5 and SunSpec Modbus reference implementations](https://open-satori.org) | open | 4 | IEEE 2030.5 / CSIP client with a SunSpec Modbus bridge that connects inverters, batteries and EVs to utility programs without firmware changes. pip install py20305; code at github.com/DERSecurity/py20305 (Apache-2.0). Satori Scout, the free iOS/Android reference app, handles device discovery, simulation and VPP connectivity (source under commercial license). |
| `gridappsd-2030-5` | [GRIDAPPS-D IEEE 2030.5 repositories](https://github.com/GRIDAPPSD) | open | 4 | Go components for IEEE 2030.5 server, client and inverter simulator. Repository existence only; conformance not checked. |

# Track 4: Aggregate distributed compute

> Aggregate distributed compute to make it grid-friendly.

Theme link: grid-friendly compute is coordinated across sites so the grid can rely on it. See [theme](../../guides/theme/README.md).

## 1. The problem

How can many small compute sites act as one resource for the grid? That needs a way to receive
grid signals, decide which sites respond, move work between sites, meter and prove what was
delivered, and meet market or program rules.

## 2. Facts that shape this track

| # | Fact | Source id |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | FERC Order 2222 requires organized markets to accept DER aggregations; minimum size up to 100 kW; not ERCOT | `ferc-2222`, `ferc-2222-fact-sheet` |
| 2 | CAISO aggregations need utility concurrence (30 business days), a scheduling coordinator and revenue-quality meters | `caiso-der-provider`, `caiso-demand-response` |
| 3 | MISO demand response minimums: 0.1 MW (LMR), 1 MW (DRR); up to 16 dispatches a year | `miso-lmr-faq` |
| 4 | North America had about 33 GW of VPPs; DOE scenario 80 to 160 GW by 2030 | `doe-vpp-announcement-2025` |
| 5 | OpenADR 3 is a public REST/OpenAPI spec; certification is separate | `openadr` |
| 6 | Equal MW does not give equal reliability; capacity credit depends on timing and duration | `doe-resource-adequacy-2024` |
| 7 | Edge applications need mobility and discovery across sites with intermittent links | `etsi-edge-native-2023` |

## 3. Your loop in this track

| Loop part | Options in the catalog |
|---|---|
| Data | `caiso-dmm-dr-2024`, `cec-dsgs-docket` (storage VPP performance), `eia-930`, `peeringdb`, workload traces (Track 3) |
| Verifier | `citylearn`, `helics`, `gridlab-d`, `vessim` |
| Coordination platforms | `lfe-flexmeasures` (by [Seita](https://seita.nl/), Nicolas Höning), `lfe-shapeshifter`, `lfe-hyphae`, `lfe-geisa` (LF Energy) |
| Protocols | `openadr`, `openleadr`, `lfe-cupid`, `ieee-2030-5`, `open-satori` (open-source 2030.5 client by DERSec), `gridappsd-2030-5` |
| Metric | Aggregate MW available, delivered vs committed, response time, minimum size met |
| Proposer | A model or policy that assigns grid requests to sites |

## 4. Outputs that demo well

| # | Format |
|---|---|
| 1 | Dashboard: grid signal in, sites responding, total MW delivered vs requested |
| 2 | Map of sites with live status |
| 3 | Delivery accuracy across loop iterations |

| `ocpp` | [OCPP: Open Charge Point Protocol (Open Charge Alliance)](https://openchargealliance.org/protocols/open-charge-point-protocol/) | verified | standard | 3 | Open protocol between EV chargers and charging management systems, including smart charging profiles that cap or schedule charging power. |
| `openadr` | [OpenADR 3.0](https://www.openadr.org/openadr-3-0) | verified | standard | 3 | REST/OpenAPI standard for DR, price and DER signals; public YAML spec supplements 2.0a/b. Reference implementation is members-only; certification is separate from implementing the API. |
| `lfe-ores` | [ORES: Open Renewable Energy Systems](https://lfenergy.org/projects/ores-open-renewable-energy-systems/) | verified | standard | 3 | Open standards and practice for plug-and-play microgrids and grid-interactive device metadata and APIs. LF Energy stage: Sandbox. Code: github.com/open-renewable-energy-systems. |
| `pge-rule-24` | [PG&E Rule 24 (third-party demand response)](https://www.pge.com/en/save-energy-and-money/energy-saving-programs/demand-response-programs/rule-24.html) | verified | program | 3 | Customers enroll with third-party DR providers that bid aggregated reductions into CAISO. |
| `sce-cbp-elect` | [SCE Capacity Bidding Program Elect](https://www.sce.com/save-money/savings-programs/enroll-in-savings-programs/capacity-bidding-program-elect) | verified | program | 3 | Pays participants for temporary reductions during high demand; overlap restrictions with other DR programs. |
| `sce-elrp` | [SCE Emergency Load Reduction Program](https://www.sce.com/factsheet/emergency-load-reduction-program) | verified | program | 3 | Seven-year DR pilot 2021 to 2027 for qualifying non-residential customers, including CCA and Direct Access. |
| `sunspec-specifications` | [SunSpec specifications and certification](https://sunspec.org/specifications/) | verified | standard | 3 | SunSpec Alliance specifications for DER communication (SunSpec Modbus, IEEE 2030.5/CSIP test specs, security). Certification programs and test labs: https://sunspec.org/certifications/. |
| `open-eac-alliance` | [OpenEAC Alliance M&V methodologies](https://github.com/wattcarbon/open-eac-alliance) |  | standard | 3 | Open, peer-reviewed measurement and verification (M&V) methodologies for issuing Energy Attribute Certificates (EACs) per watt-hour or gram CO2e from battery storage, electrification, demand response and energy efficiency projects. Methods and statuses at methods.openeac.org; drafts go through a 30-day public comment period. |
